question: How did neural machine translation develop from statistical methods to transformer based systems?

2602.17287.caption: The figure consists of six line plots arranged in two rows and three columns, showing metrics (Average Cosine Similarity, Rényi Entropy, and Spherical Variance) plotted against Checkpoint steps for various model configurations. The top row displays metrics for decoder output, decoder embeddings, and encoder outputs, while the bottom row displays the same metrics specifically for encoder outputs. The plots compare "Transformer-big" and "Transformer-base" models against their counterparts augmented with R(E), illustrating how these metrics evolve during training.

2604.25702.caption: The figure is a flowchart consisting of text labels, icons, and decision diamonds connected by arrows. It depicts a process where "text" is processed by an "expert translator" to produce "translated text," followed by a decision diamond asking "is the set large enough?" which leads to either a termination or a loop that adds "the rejected preferred answer pairs to the set."

2603.17087.caption: The figure is a line graph plotting BLEU score on the y-axis against training steps on the x-axis. It contains two colored lines with corresponding legends representing the translation directions EN$\rightarrow$PL (blue) and PL$\rightarrow$EN (orange), conveying the learning progress and performance convergence of the Llama-3.2-1B model over 20,000 training steps.

1509.08644.caption: The figure displays a horizontal color-coded scale labeled "Fig. 1. BLEU interpretability scale," ranging from 20 to 70. The scale uses a gradient from red (20) to yellow (40) to green (70) to represent different levels of BLEU score interpretability.

2109.01396.caption: The figure consists of two side-by-side line plots with x-axes labeled "number of batches" ranging from 0 to 80k. The left plot shows "avg. src contribution" increasing and then plateauing, while the right plot shows "entropy" increasing and then decreasing, with vertical dashed lines separating different training stages. Together, the plots convey how the contribution and entropy of source information evolve through the different stages of the NMT training process.

2002.06546.caption: The figure consists of two panels, (a) Training and (b) Decoding, illustrating a separable attention mechanism between target and source representations across two layers. Each panel uses grids of black dots to represent hidden states at different layers ($i$ and $i+1$) and time steps ($S$ for source, $T$ for target), with colored arrows (green for target-to-source and blue for source-to-target) showing the flow of information between layers. The diagrams convey how the model jointly attends to source and target representations to facilitate translation between Chinese pinyin and English.

1608.04631.caption: This line graph plots the percentage of translation error rate (%mTER) on the y-axis against sentence length ranges (1-15, 16-25, 26-35, and >35) on the x-axis. It compares four translation models—PBSY, HPB, SPB, and NMT—showing that mTER scores increase for all models as sentence length increases, with the NMT model consistently maintaining the lowest error rates across all length bins.

1706.09733.caption: The figure consists of five line graphs and one table comparing the performance of Adam and SGD optimizers across different translation tasks. Each graph plots BLEU scores against the number of training sentences, using orange diamonds for Adam and blue squares for SGD, with vertical dotted lines marking two Adam restarts. The accompanying table lists the final dev set perplexities for both optimizers across the five datasets (DE-EN, EN-FI, RO-EN, EN-FR, and CS-EN).

2308.10482.caption: The figure provides a schematic overview of the PhraseTransformer (CrossH) architecture, comparing a standard Transformer Encoder to the proposed model. It illustrates how the Multi-Head Attention layer is modified with a "Phrase Integration" block, which utilizes $n$-gram LSTM layers to process input sequences into phrase representations. The diagram uses boxes to represent neural layers and vectors, with arrows indicating data flow from input embeddings through positional encoding and multi-head attention mechanisms.

1804.06189.caption: The figure consists of four line graphs sharing a common x-axis labeled "# size (million of sentences)," representing the training data size for two datasets: "authentic" (solid line) and "hybrid" (dashed line). The y-axes plot different NMT quality metrics: TER (where lower is better), METEOR, and CHRF1 (where higher is better). The plots convey how translation quality evolves as training data increases, showing that the hybrid dataset generally outperforms the authentic dataset across all metrics.

2008.07772.caption: The figure illustrates the architecture of a Transformer model, consisting of two main components: an encoder (left) and a decoder (right). Each component is composed of stacked sub-layers, including Multi-Head Attention and Feed Forward networks, connected by residual connections and layer normalization (Add & Norm) blocks. The diagram uses boxes to represent functional modules and arrows to indicate the flow of data from input embeddings through the stacked layers to the final output probabilities.

1704.04743.caption: The figure displays two hierarchical tree structures representing translations of a German sentence into English, with blue lines connecting source words to target words. The top part shows a lexicalized constituency tree predicted by the bpe2tree model, while the bottom part shows a linearized translation from the bpe2bpe model, with the blue lines illustrating the attention-induced word alignments for each model.
